power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p > 0.3", "p > 0.39", "p > 0.15", "p > 0.12" ), Sentence = c("Indeed, per Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests, none of the distributions for any of the latent variables significantly differed from uniform (all p > 0.3, FDR-corrected for 12 tests).", "Again, none of the distributions for any of the latent variables significantly differed from uniform (all p > 0.39, FDR corrected for 16 tests).", "In keeping with the simulation parameters, wsPLSC identified one of the four latent variables as significant (p < 0.001; all other p > 0.15).", "In keeping with the simulation parameters, wsPLSC identified one of the 4 latent variables as significant (p < 0.001; all other p > 0.12)." )), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Partial least squares correlation (PLSC) is a multivariate technique used in neuroscience to capture patterns of relationships between neural data and covariates of interest.
Conventionally, PLSC captures between-subjects correlations (e.g., between average neural activation and average task performance).
However, within-subject correlations (e.g., trial-by-trial relationships between neural activation and subjective ratings or stimulus attributes) are often of interest as well.
Thus, we introduce an extension of PLSC to capture within-subject correlations.
We validate this approach against related parametric methods and demonstrate that it detects known effects in simulated data and reproduces published findings in open fMRI and EEG datasets.
This method is freely available as part of the pyplsc and mne-plsc Python packages.

Partial least squares correlation (PLSC) is a multivariate analytic technique used in chemometrics (for a review, see Mehmood and Ahmed, 2016) and neuroscience (via the PLS software package; McIntosh et al., 1996; McIntosh and Lobaugh, 2004; Krishnan et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Partial least squares correlation (PLSC) is a multivariate analytic technique used in chemometrics (for a review, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Mehmood and Ahmed, 2016)</ref> and neuroscience (via the PLS software package; <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">McIntosh et al., 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">McIntosh and Lobaugh, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Krishnan et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: It uses singular value decomposition (SVD) to explain relationships among a large number of observed variables using a small number of latent variables.

In this way it is conceptually similar to principal component analysis (PCA): whereas PCA captures the total variance in a dataset, PLSC captures the covariance between a main set of multivariate observations and a smaller set of covariates.
Existing PLSC methods are applicable when the unit of observation is coarser than individual trials.
That is, they capture covariance between participant-level multivariate neural data (averaged over trials) and participant-level covariates (e.g., questionnaire scores or average task performance).
However, research questions can often pertain to within-subject correlations.
For example, we may be interested in the trialby-trial relationship between neural data and subjective ratings or stimulus attributes.
Importantly, trialby-trial relationships can disappear or even reverse when trial-level measurements are averaged, as they are in conventional PLSC.
This phenomenon, known as "Simpson's paradox", has been demonstrated in for functional connectivity estimates, which often differ at the within-versus between-subjects level (Roberts et al., 2016).
text.formatted: This phenomenon, known as "Simpson's paradox", has been demonstrated in for functional connectivity estimates, which often differ at the within-versus between-subjects level <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Roberts et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, evaluating within-subjects correlations requires extending existing PLSC methods.
In this paper, we introduce and validate a novel extension of PLSC for within-subjects correlations (henceforth wsPLSC), which we have made freely available as part of the pyplsc Python package.

This method is applicable to multivariate data in general (and pyplsc is modality-agnostic, operating directly on matrices and data frames), but in this paper we will focus on neuroscience using both the M/EEG-specific Python package mne-plsc and the more general pyplsc for fMRI.
Before describing wsPLSC, we first review the mathematics of the conventional between-subjects PLSC method.

Consider a set of N obs observations of N var neural data variables (e.g., voltage at a specific time and electrode, BOLD signal at a specific time and voxel) organized in a matrix X and a set of N obs observations of N cov covariates (e.g., behavioural measures, where typically N cov < N var ) organized in a matrix Y .
text.formatted: Consider a set of N obs observations of N var neural data variables (e.g., voltage at a specific time and electrode, BOLD signal at a specific time and voxel) organized in a matrix X and a set of N obs observations of N cov covariates (e.g., behavioural measures, where typically N cov < N var ) organized in a matrix Y .

text.text: X has dimensions (N obs , N var ) and Y has dimensions (N obs , N cov ).

The cross-correlation R between X and Y can be computed by first normalizing each column (subtracting the mean and dividing by the L2 norm) and then taking the matrix product: R = Y T X (1) yielding a matrix with dimensions (N cov , N var ).

R can then be submitted to compact SVD, which yields a triplet of matrices U , S, and V : R = U T SV where the columns of U and V are the left and right singular vectors, respectively (analogous to the eigenvectors of PCA), and S is a diagonal matrix containing the singular values (analogous to the eigenvalues of PCA).

Within neuroscience applications of PLSC, the left singular vectors in U are referred to as the "design saliences", and the right singular vectors in V as the "brain saliences" for reasons that will become clear shortly.
SVD can be understood as identifying a set of latent variables (LVs) that explain the correlations between neural variables and covariates.
The number of latent variables is equal to the rank of R, and is thus typically equal to N cov .
Each latent variable is represented by a triplet of (1) a set of brain saliences, (2) a set of design saliences, and (3) a singular value.

The brain and design saliences represent weights that can be used to compute linear combinations of neural variables and covariates, and the strength of the correlation between these linear combinations is captured by the singular value.
As in PCA, singular values are ordered by magnitude such that the first latent variable captures the most cross-correlation and subsequent latent variables capture less and less.

In PLSC, statistical inference occurs via permutation testing, in which the rows of Y are repeatedly shuffled at random with respect to the rows of X and the SVD of their cross-correlation is re-computed.
This breaks any systematic relationship between the neural variables and covariates and yields a null distribution of singular values for each latent variable.

If the observed singular value for a given latent variable is above the 95th percentile of its null distribution, that latent variable is considered to explain statistically significant amount of the cross correlation between the neural variables and the covariates.

Having identified a singificant latent variable, we often want to characterize the associated brain saliences to determine which specific neural variables contribute strongly to a multivariate pattern related to one or more covariates.
To do so, we can use bootstrap resampling to estimate the standard deviation of the brain saliences and compute z scores by dividing each observed brain salience by its standard deviation.
Conventionally, brain saliences with |z| > 2 are considered stable and important contributors to a latent variable.
text.formatted: Conventionally, brain saliences with |z| > 2 are considered stable and important contributors to a latent variable.

text.text: It is also possible to simplify interpretation by performing cluster analysis on the brain saliences, such that only large groups of stable saliences that are adjacent in space, time, or frequency are interpreted (see, for example, Wiebels et al., 2016).
text.formatted: It is also possible to simplify interpretation by performing cluster analysis on the brain saliences, such that only large groups of stable saliences that are adjacent in space, time, or frequency are interpreted (see, for example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Wiebels et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: When observations are stratified by between-or within-subjects conditions, cross-correlation matrices are computed for each condition and "stacked" vertically to form a matrix R with N obs × N conds rows and N cov columns (where N conds is the number of experimental conditions).
Note that the "direction" of stacking is a matter of convention and is mathematically arbitrary.
By decomposing this stacked matrix, PLSC can capture both overall patterns of cross-correlation and their modulation by experimental condition.

Conventional PLSC can be extended to within-subjects correlations by computing cross-correlation matrices over trials within participants (stratifying by within-subjects conditions as applicable), averaging these participant-specific matrices (stratifying by between-subjects conditions as applicable), and performing SVD on the resulting final matrix, which has N obs × N conds rows and N cov columns.
Participant-specific correlation coefficients can be normalized via an arctanh transform prior to averaging (Fisher, 1915) and re-scaled afterward via a tanh transform.
text.formatted: Participant-specific correlation coefficients can be normalized via an arctanh transform prior to averaging <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Fisher, 1915)</ref> and re-scaled afterward via a tanh transform.

text.text: Formally, the rows of X and Y correspond to individual trials in wsPLSC.
Let X subj and Y subj be the trial-level neural data and covariates for a given participant.
We can compute a participant-specific crosscorrelation matrix R subj by z-scoring each column of X subj and Y subj and taking the matrix product:
These subject-specific matrices are arctanh transformed, averaged together, and re-scaled via a tanh transform to arrive at the final matrix: which is then submitted to SVD.
As in conventional PLSC, the statistical significance of latent variables can be assessed via permutation testing and the stability of brain saliences can be assessed by bootstrap resampling.

Both permutation and bootstrapping must be stratified, accounting for the clustered nature of the data (i.e., participants are nested in between-subjects conditions; within-subjects conditions are nested in participants; trials are nested in within-subjects conditions).
This is already the case in conventional PLSC, and is extended to the level of individual trials for wsPLSC.
For example, individual trial-level covariates (i.e., rows of Y ) would be shuffled within participants or within-subject condition labels, as applicable.

The product of the brain saliences for a latent variable k (i.e., the kth column of V denoted by V * k ) with the neural data X is referred to as the "brain scores" B k for that latent variable: which summarizes how strongly the multivariate patterns captured by the brain saliences are expressed for each observation.

The correlations between these brain scores and the covariates are useful for characterizing the latent variable and are often visualized (with quantile-based confidence intervals from bootstrap resampling) in conventional PLSC analyses.
In wsPLSC, we can similarly visualize the within-subjects correlations between the brain scores and the covariates.
In the remainder of this paper, we will attempt to validate and demonstrate wsPLSC.

We will aim to show that wsPLSC (1) produces similar results to a conceptually similar parametric method for univariate data, (2) has appropriate type-I error rates, (3) detects simulated effects, and (4) reproduces established results for a public dataset.
Analyses used the pyplsc and mne-plsc Python libraries, under Python 3.12.4.
Analysis scripts are available at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.34872573.

To overcome the sign ambiguity inherent to SVD, bootstrap resamples were aligned via a procrustes rotation of the design saliences applied to the brain saliences (in keeping with the approach used in the original Matlab PLS software; McIntosh and Lobaugh, 2004).

text.text: First, we compared wsPLSC to conventional between-subjects PLSC in order to demonstrate the fundamental difference between the two methods.
In principle, within-subjects correlations are independent from betweensubjects correlations.
In the extreme, they can even be opposite to one another, a phenomenon known as "Simpson's paradox" (Simpson, 1951).
text.formatted: In the extreme, they can even be opposite to one another, a phenomenon known as "Simpson's paradox" <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Simpson, 1951)</ref>.

text.text: For illustrative purposes, we simulated a Simpson-paradoxical dataset in which a latent variable exhibited opposite correlations to a covariate at the between-versus within-subjects level.
The goal of this simulation was to demonstrate that, in principle, wsPLSC is not redundant with conventional between-subjects PLSC.
Nonetheless, while we do not simulate this possibility here, the two methods can also yield matching results.
We simulated data for 5 "participants" who each completed 20 "trials".

On each trial, a single covariate c was simulated using two components: an participant-wise component c participant (simulated as a normal random variable with variance 3 and shared across all trials for a given participant) and a trial-wise component c trial (simulated as a standard normal random variable separately for each trial):

Multivariate data d for 100 variables were simulated using to a single set of weights w shared across all participants, which were generated as standard normal variables and multiplied with the two components of c:
The trial-level data were submitted directly to wsPLSC analysis, whereas we first averaged observations within participants before submitting these to conventional between-subjects PLSC analysis.
SVD can be applied to scalar values and column vectors, meaning that PLSC can be applied to unvariate data (with a single outcome variable and a single covariate).

Conceptually, univariate wsPLSC aims to detect the same effects as a linear mixed effects model (LMM) that models a single continuous outcome variable, a single continuous predictor, possibly several categorical predictors, and a participant-level random intercept.
Thus, if the stratified permutation approach used to assess significance in wsPLSC is valid, univariate wsPLSC should produce results similar to those of LMMs.
To evaluate whether this is the case, we simulated a series of experiments for analysis via both methods.
We first performed a set of simulations in which observations were not stratified by any experimental condition.
We simulated 100 experiments, each with 50 "participants" who each completed 100 "trials".
We first simulated participant-level random intercepts as standard normal random variates.

Then, for each participant, a single observed variable and a single covariate were simulated: the observed variable was simulated as the sum of the relevant participant-level intercept and a standard normal random variable, and the covariate was simply simulated as a standard normal random variable.
For each experiment, a wsPLSC model and an LMM were fit to to the data.

text.text: For each LMM, the p value associated with the effect of the covariate was extracted for comparison with the corresponding p value produced by wsPLSC via permutation testing (since the data from each experiment consisted of only one observed variable and one covariate, each wsPLSC analysis yielded only one latent variable and thus one p value).
In a second set of simulations, we introduced two between-subjects conditions and two within-subjects conditions.

We again simulated 100 experiments, each with 50 participants per between-subjects condition (for 60 participants total), who each completed 100 trials per within-subjects condition (for 200 trials total per participant).
For each experiment, we first simulated fixed effects of within-and between-subjects conditions as standard normal random variates.
We also simulated participant-level random intercepts as standard normal random variates.

For a given trial for a given participant, the covariate was simply simulated as a standard normal random variable, and the observed variable was simulated as a standard normal random variable plus the relevant within-and between-subjects fixed effects and the participant-level random intercept.
When analyzing this second set of experiments using wsPLSC, the stacked cross-correlations formed a column vector of length 4 (the number of combinations of within-and between-subjects conditions).
SVD of this column vector again yielded one singular value, and thus permution testing produced one p value.

To obtain parametric p values for comparison, we first fit a full LMM for each experiment via the formula: where obs refers to the observed variable, cov refers to the covariate, and within and between refer to the within-and between-subjects condition labels, respectively.

We compared this full model via likelihood ratio tests with the following reduced model: which included terms for within-and between-subjects conditions because PLSC captures the effect of a covariate and its interaction with experimental conditions, but does not capture differences in observed variables by experimental condition per se.

Importantly, in both sets of simulated data, there was no systematic relationship between the covariate and the outcome variable in any experimental condition, nor any systematic difference in this relationship across conditions.
Thus, p values for both mixed effects models and wsPLSC should be uniformly distributed between 0 and 1 and linearly related.
In multivariate data, with many observed variables and relatively few observations, spurious cross-correlations will inevitably appear by chance even in the absence of true underlying relationships.

Because SVD systematically identifies the pairs of observed variables and covariates that are maximally correlated with one another, a potential concern is that wsPLSC might identify spurious cross-correlations as significant and therefore suffer from an inflated type-I error rate.

If wsPLSC is statistically valid (i.e., if it has an appropriate type-1 error rate), then under the null hypothesis of no systematic relationship between any covariate and any observed variable, the p value distribution should be uniform (i.e., p < 0.01 1% of the time, p < 0.05 5% of the time, etc.).

We first simulated multivariate data for 1000 experiments in which 5 "participants" each completed 20 "trials". 10,000 observed variables and 12 covariates were simulated.
As in the univariate simulations, each observed variable had a participant-level random intercept simulated as a standard normal random variate.
Observations were not stratified by any experimental conditions.
Thus, the cross-correlation matrix submitted to SVD had 12 rows and 10,000 columns, yielding 12 singular values and thus 12 p values per experiment.
We collected these p values to determine whether, for each of the 12 pairs of latent variables, the p values followed a uniform distribution.
We next stimulated a second set of 1000 experiments with 5 participants per each of two betweensubjects conditions, who each completed 20 trials per each of two within-subjects conditions.
For ease of visualization (to avoid producing a large number of p values per experiment), 10,000 observed variables but only 4 covariates were simulated.
As in the univariate case, observed variables included participant-level random intercepts as well as fixed effects of within-and between-subjects conditions.
Each experiment yielded 16 p values (4 covariates × 2 within-subjects conditions × 2 between-subjects conditions).
For both sets of experiments, we used Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests to determine whether the observed distribution of p values differed significantly from a uniform distribution.

We applied FDR correction to the results of these distributional tests (i.e., to the p values from the Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests, not to the p values directly obtained from wsPLSC), given that there were 12 tests in the first set of simulations and 16 tests in the second set of simulations.
We next simulated both an fMRI and an EEG experiment with two covariates and two within-subjects experimental conditions.

In the "positive" condition, a "positive covariate" was correlated with the amplitude of the hemodynamic response function (HRF) in the fMRI experiment and with the amplitude of an eventrelated potential (ERP) in the EEG experiment, whereas a "null covariate" was not.

Although these results were possible to obtain in the original datasets via alternative methods, wsPLSC offers a conceptually elegant method that is already familiar to many neuroscience researchers (McIntosh and Lobaugh, 2004).

Traditional ERP analysis involves analyzing amplitude at some channel or set of channels of interest, at some latency or within some temporal window of interest.

In PLSC, we can perform a similar analysis via spatiotemporal clustering: after defining an adjacency matrix over channels and times, clusters of adjacent brain saliences with z-scores above some threshold (conventionally |z| > 2, but higher thresholds can be used to avoid overly broad clusters; for the current analysis, we used a threshold of |z| > 5).

We have introduced a novel extension to PLSC to capture within-subject correlations, which we refer to as wsPLSC.

We have demonstrated that wsPLSC yields comparable results to conceptually similar parametric methods for univariate data; exhibits an appropriate type-I error rate for multivariate data; and can detect both known effects in simulated data and published results in a public dataset. wsPLSC is available as part of the open-source pyplsc package and can be applied to M/EEG data via the mne-plsc package.
A major advantage of within-subjects analysis is its specificity.

Multivariate methods exist for analyzing condition-wise differences (e.g., "mean-centred" PLSC or barycentric discriminant analysis; Krishnan et al., 2011; Abdi et al., 2018), and condition-wise differences are often interpreted in terms of the presence versus absence of some underlying variable that could also be treated as a covariate.

text.text: For example, a contrast between painful vs neutral stimuli conditions can be interpreted as a signature of subjective pain (Wager et al., 2013).
text.formatted: For example, a contrast between painful vs neutral stimuli conditions can be interpreted as a signature of subjective pain <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Wager et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, an analysis that is able to compare condition-wise differences against correlations with an underlying covariate can provide valuable insight into the nature of the construct being studied.
For example, in a study of mental imagery, is the difference between an imagery versus a perception condition similar to the pattern associated with subjective vividness ratings?
In a study of memory, is the pattern associated with successful recognition similar to the pattern associated with subjective familiarity?
In a study of pain, is the difference between painful versus neutral stimuli similar to the pattern correlated with subjective pain ratings?
By addressing questions such as these, wsPLSC can be a useful complement to existing methods.
It is important to note that we do not claim wsPLSC is necessarily superior to other analytic techniques for examining within-subjects correlations.

Nonetheless, PLSC more broadly does offer advantages as an open-ended ombnibus technique that does not require the researcher to pre-specify the variables where an effect is likely to be found (i.e., ROIs or times/frequency bands of interest).
It is thus particularly wellsuited to exploratory analyses that cannot be constrained by the existing literature, and wsPLSC inherits these advantages.

We therefore believe that wsPLSC will be a useful extension to PLSC for researchers familiar with this analytic approach and its conventions, and for those investigating more exploratory research questions.
